title: Cabinet Extends 850 Fast-Track Courts for Rape and POCSO Cases to 2031
excerpt: The Union Cabinet has approved five more years for the Fast Track Special Courts scheme, expanding it from 779 to 850 courts with a total outlay of Rs 3,788.04 crore, the central share paid from the Nirbhaya Fund.
body:
• The Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved continuing the Fast Track Special Courts scheme for five more years, from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2031, for the expeditious trial of rape and POCSO cases.
  • The scheme will grow from 779 functional courts today — including 399 exclusive POCSO courts — to 850 courts, with additional districts chosen on the basis of case pendency.
  • The total outlay is Rs 3,788.04 crore: a central share of Rs 2,353.15 crore funded from the Nirbhaya Fund, and Rs 1,434.89 crore from states and Union Territories.
  • Since the scheme began on October 2, 2019, these courts have disposed of 4,02,457 cases, according to the government release. Each court is staffed with a dedicated judicial officer and a special public prosecutor.

India specialised courts for sexual offence trials will run for at least five more years. The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has approved the continuation of the centrally sponsored scheme for Fast Track Special Courts (FTSCs), including exclusive POCSO courts, for a further five years from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2031, according to the government release published by the Press Information Bureau. The scheme carries a total financial outlay of Rs 3,788.04 crore, with the central share of Rs 2,353.15 crore funded from the Nirbhaya Fund and the remaining Rs 1,434.89 crore borne by states and Union Territories.

More courts, chosen by backlog

The renewed scheme provides for 850 FTSCs, up from the 779 functional today, of which 399 are exclusive POCSO courts. The expansion is intended to reach additional districts, which will be identified on the basis of the pendency of rape and POCSO Act cases, the release said. Each court is provided with a dedicated judicial officer, a special public prosecutor and support staff, so that the cases are heard by a bench that does nothing else. The JK Post reported the same approval, announced at Wednesday Cabinet briefing.

The record so far

The scheme has been operational since October 2, 2019, launched in pursuance of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2018 and in compliance with Supreme Court directions of July 25, 2019. Since inception, the courts have disposed of 4,02,457 cases, according to the release. Those disposal figures are the government own measure of the scheme; what they do not show is how long the cases that remain pending have been waiting, which is the number survivors and their families experience directly.

What to watch

Because the scheme is centrally sponsored, the expansion to 850 courts depends on participating states setting up the additional courts and staffing them. The pace at which the new districts are notified and the judges appointed will decide whether the five-year extension changes trial timelines on the ground, or simply keeps the existing 779 courts funded. State notifications and Department of Justice disposal data are the next signals to watch.
